title: Otto Vass jurors face difficult task
article: Juries can sometimes shock and confound in their verdicts.

Declaring O.J. Simpson an innocent man comes most immediately to mind. But I recall also a local case from many years back, when a young mother accused of killing her baby was acquitted of murder even though she'd led police to the rural spot where the child's remains were found, claiming she'd seen it in a dream. It was the traumatized woman's emotional pain that moved the jurors to mercy, despite her palpable guilt.

There is much pain - and anger - that lingers over the acquittal in 2003 of four Toronto officers on manslaughter charges in the death of mentally ill _Otto_ _Vass_. But that jury was clearly convinced that the constables had responded with justifiable force to a demonstrably violent individual who'd spent the previous 12 hours causing havoc and wreckage at every turn - from jumping out of his vehicle in traffic, because he believed a bomb was planted under the seat, to an unprovoked sock in the head of an innocent bystander outside a convenience store, to the enraged punch to the face of a cop questioning him following a completely peaceful verbal exchange. A juror would later write to one of the officers "It was a week ago today that I and eleven other jurors found you and the other three officers 'not guilty' in the _Otto_ _Vass_ trial. We suggested to Mr. (Patrick) LeSage after our verdict that this case should never have gone to trial resulting in 3 agonizing years. It should have been a 'coroner's inquest' and nothing more."
Copies of this and a similar note were obtained by the Star last night, as the coroner's inquest finally went to the jury after four weeks of testimony.

To balance this view of the tragic events that occurred in the early morning hours of Aug. 9, 2000, I will quote from a release issued yesterday by the Committee for Justice for _Otto_ _Vass_ "Do you believe the high priced lawyers of the four police officers - the lawyers who received hundreds of thousands of dollars for their efforts in, successfully, getting the four police officers acquitted?" And, further "The strategy was to portray _Vass_ as a mentally unstable individual who brought the attack on himself. And it was a strategy that clearly worked." Also "Too much of the defence of the police reduced itself to demonizing _Vass_ as a 'mentally unstable' danger to society. We have to insist that those with a mental health history are judged by the same standards as those without. Being labelled 'mentally ill' should not be a death sentence."

Agreed. But the officers who wrangled with _Vass_ that night - he was struck by at least 15 blows (that left a mark), although some of these could be attributed to a pal of the injured bystander who confronted _Vass_ inside the store immediately afterwards - knew nothing about his medical history and were simply responding to a 911 call. They did not initiate the violence. And they continued to hit the heavy-set _Vass_, they told the inquest, because he was powerfully resisting arrest.

_Vass_ was clearly frightened of the police and, as persuasively conjectured by a lawyer for the Empowerment Council - a community group with expertise in mental health and police training - likely terrified he would again be put into a restraint, perhaps institutionalized. But the fear cut both ways.

"Fear is a factor whenever our clients and police interact," Anita Szigeti told the jury. "My suggestion is that _Otto_ _Vass_ threw the first punch because he was frightened they would take him to the hospital against his will, forcibly restrained, physically and chemically. The only thing that could have prevented this (incident) from happening was removing the fear. It was a reciprocal fear."
But Szigeti was seriously off the mark when she also made this observation "The fact he had mental health problems did not make him more prone to violence than anyone else."

_Vass_ had a long history of dramatic violence, induced by his bipolar illness, including kicking a nurse unconscious and setting a house on fire after locking in the occupants. None of this was his moral fault. It was, catastrophically, in his nature at those times when he was seized by volatile, delusional episodes.

The soft tissue injuries _Vass_ suffered were not severe enough to directly cause death. But die he did, at the end of a three-and-a- half minute pounding. Originally, a coroner determined that there was no anatomical or toxicological cause of death. Some months later he revised that opinion so that formal cause of death was ascribed to a fat embolism - a sliver of fat dislodged by the blows, released into his lungs, bringing on suffocation.

It is a rare, even exotic, finding. Moreover, at trial and in this inquest, it was heavily disputed by experts. Even the pathologist of record, Dr. David Chiasson, told this jury death could have resulted from a combination of multiple factors including stress, excited delirium, the victim's enlarged heart and morbid obesity, or restraint asphyxia.

In some ways, the criminal jury had it easier. They were not required to pronounce on cause of death. This jury, after listening to conflicting evidence from expert pathologists, must make a medical-legal evaluation; to decide whether the death was natural, accidental, a homicide or "undetermined."

Homicide does not mean the same thing in coroner's court as it does in criminal court. Here, it's defined as "the action of a human being killing another human being." Juries are not permitted to apportion blame. Their conclusions are based on "a balance of probabilities," rather than the more exacting "beyond a reasonable doubt."

Whatever the definition, homicide carries a mighty wallop outside the court. In his charge to the jury, coroner Dr. William Lucas reminded them of that. "It's a neutral (word) that does not reflect culpability or blame. However, we must acknowledge that a finding of homicide may have significant consequences for those involved and it may carry a stigma."
Peter Rosenthal, representing one of _Vass_'s sons, told the jury this "Would he have died without human interaction? It's inconceivable."
Cause of death - human interaction. Try putting that on a death certificate.
Rosie DiManno usually appears Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday.
